nodes.name: DG32-LITE AI Compute Envelope (No Accelerator)
nodes.communityName: 30 Industrial Edge AI Use Cases & Scalar DSP
nodes.description: Physical execution envelope for lightweight edge AI on a 50 MHz RV32IM scalar core. DG32-LITE executes machine learning tasks without an attention engine using a proven scalar hierarchy: 12.5 MMAC/s throughput, 16.5 KB model budget, 82% free CPU cycles, and CORDIC hardware math.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator (Sept 2026) — Slide 01 & 03

nodes.name: Thirty Industrial Use Cases on Scalar Core
nodes.communityName: 30 Industrial Edge AI Use Cases & Scalar DSP
nodes.description: Comprehensive catalogue of 30 predictive diagnostics and control tasks running on DG32-LITE. Four groups of industrial AI workloads that run natively on DG32-LITE without an attention engine, spanning rotating machinery, electrical motor current signature analysis, real-time control, and long-term degradation.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slides 05–10

nodes.name: Tree Ensembles & The 19-Model Hierarchy
nodes.communityName: 30 Industrial Edge AI Use Cases & Scalar DSP
nodes.description: Why zero-multiply decision trees and linear models outperform deep neural networks on microcontrollers. On a scalar CPU without a MAC array, comparisons and table lookups cost almost nothing. A 100-tree random forest at depth 8 requires roughly 800 comparisons and zero multiplications, running in 0.06 ms at >1 kHz.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slides 04–05

nodes.name: Feature Extraction & CORDIC Demodulation
nodes.communityName: 30 Industrial Edge AI Use Cases & Scalar DSP
nodes.description: Costed signal-processing front-end: envelope demodulation, Goertzel filters, and kurtosis rules. The diagnostic front-end reuses CORDIC hardware already present for motor control (Park/Clarke/magnitude/atan2 in <20 cycles). Demodulated features evaluated at known physical fault frequencies outrank raw moments by 4–5×.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slide 06

nodes.name: AFE Sensing Constraints & ISO Standards
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Why the analog front end, not compute or RAM, is the true binding constraint in motor diagnostics. ISO 13373-2 defines usable dynamic range as D = 6(N-1) dB. For an 8-bit ADC, dynamic range is only 42 dB, while broken rotor bar sidebands sit -40 to -60 dBc below the fundamental, disappearing under the quantization floor.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slide 11

nodes.name: CWRU Benchmark Audit & Advisory ML Boundary
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Academic data leakage audit and the strict advisory role of machine learning under hardware lockstep. A critical audit of academic bearing benchmarks reveals widespread data leakage: 40 of 41 published CWRU studies used leaky splits. Furthermore, ML inference on DG32-LITE operates in an advisory role only, subservient to the lockstep safety core.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Base Variant: Thirty Use Cases, No Accelerator — Slide 12

nodes.name: DG32-LITE Lockstep RISC-V MCU
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Dual-core hardware lockstep motor-control SoC for entry-level brushless drives. DG32-LITE puts a RISC-V MCU, motor-control peripherals and a hardware lockstep safety monitor on one 130 nm chip. First silicon rides the September 2026 shuttle.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE Datasheet v1.0 & dr.deepgridsemi.com

nodes.name: DG32-2DOM Edge Attention SoC
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Dual-core lockstep motor-control SoC plus isolated INT8 attention engine. The identical frozen control core, pinout and limits as DG32-LITE, with an added INT8 attention engine on its own 114 MHz domain for in-situ bearing anomaly and vibration diagnosis.
nodes.citation: DG32-2DOM Technical Specification & Library Deck

nodes.name: SKU-1: BLDC Motor Controller
nodes.description: High-voltage mixed-signal motor drive with FOC CORDIC hardware accelerator. High-voltage BCD motor controller integrating gate pre-drivers directly onto the chip, achieving <1 µs closed current loop latency with integrated bootstrap diodes.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 2: SKU-1 BLDC Motor

nodes.name: SKU-2: Smart-Meter SoC
nodes.description: Tamper-proof metrology SoC for the 250M National Smart Meter rollout. Dedicated 3-phase and single-phase energy measurement SoC featuring high-dynamic-range 24-bit Sigma-Delta ADCs and hardware tamper detection active even when unpowered.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 3: SKU-2 Smart Meter

nodes.name: SKU-3: Hi-Rel PMIC
nodes.description: Radiation-tolerant power management IC for defense and aerospace avionics. High-reliability power management IC capable of surviving 100V transients on 28V military avionics buses, featuring Brokaw bandgap references and DICE flip-flop state machines.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 4: SKU-3 Hi-Rel PMIC

nodes.name: SKU-4: Lockstep Safety MCU
nodes.description: ASIL-D / SIL-3 functional safety MCU with dual temporally skewed cores. Dual DGridRiscV core microcontroller with 2-clock-cycle temporal skew and spatial separation to eliminate common-cause transient faults and guarantee fail-safe behavior.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 5: SKU-4 Lockstep MCU

nodes.name: SKU-5: Robust Interface Transceiver
nodes.description: Galvanically isolated CAN-FD & RS-485 transceiver for harsh industrial buses. Rugged bus interface transceiver engineered to survive continuous electrical overstress, ground potential differences, and electromagnetic discharge on vehicular harnesses.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 6: SKU-5 Transceiver

nodes.name: SKU-6: Quad-Rail Voltage Supervisor
nodes.description: Ultra-low-jitter precision supply monitor and brownout watchtower. Autonomous analog watchdog that monitors four independent power rails simultaneously, executing clean deglitched reset generation during power brownouts.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 7: SKU-6 Supervisor

nodes.name: SKU-7: 77 GHz 4D MIMO Radar
nodes.description: High-resolution imaging radar front-end in Silicon-Germanium BiCMOS. Sovereign 4D imaging radar RF front-end combining 3 transmitter and 4 receiver channels with integrated fractional-N PLL synthesizer, resolving azimuth and elevation at 3.75 cm range accuracy.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 8: SKU-7 77GHz Radar

nodes.name: SKU-8: Rugged Display Driver & TCON
nodes.description: High-voltage column driver and timing controller for ruggedized avionics panels. Purpose-built column driver and timing controller designed specifically to replace obsolete foreign display silicon in Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) 17
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 9: SKU-8 Display Driver

nodes.name: SKU-9: SDV Zonal Gateway
nodes.description: Software-Defined Vehicle zonal controller with e-fuses and Ethernet TSN. Next-generation zonal automotive gateway combining a Gigabit Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) switch with 16 intelligent solid-state e-fuses to replace mechanical relay boxes.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 10: SKU-9 Zonal Gateway

nodes.name: Track B: D100 Tactical Drone SoC
nodes.shortName: Track B: D100 Tactical Drone S
nodes.description: Heterogeneous autonomous flight computer on an organic multi-die SiP. Heterogeneous flight navigation processor combining an ASIL-D flight controller with a 28nm Linux compute tile, running 30 Hz Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) in GNSS-denied battlefields.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 11: D100 Tactical Drone SoC

nodes.name: DeepGrid SDV Reference Platform
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: End-to-end silicon architecture for Software-Defined Vehicles. Comprehensive vehicle electronics architecture combining central cockpit compute with 4 regional zonal gateways (SKU-9), motor control (DG32/SKU-1), and perception radar (SKU-7).
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 12: DG SDV Platform

nodes.name: The 198-Day Silicon Shuttle Loop
nodes.description: Lean silicon development sprint replacing $1M legacy EDA with open-source toolchains. DeepGrid’s breakthrough 198-day tapeout-to-silicon lifecycle that slashes chip development costs from $2M+ down to $14.3K per MPW shuttle run using open-source tools.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Mature Silicon — Chapter 5: The 198-Day Silicon Loop

nodes.name: Three-Factory Sovereignty Roadmap
nodes.description: Geopolitical supply-chain insulation spanning USA, Germany, and India. A phased de-risking roadmap that starts with commercially accessible commercial fabs in friendly nations, then systematically ports hardened IP to India’s domestic Semi-Conductor Laboratory (SCL).
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Mature Silicon — Chapter 7: Three-Factory Sovereignty Roadmap

nodes.name: Defence Procurement & Legal Moats
nodes.description: Statutory protections under DAP-2020, Make-II, and PIL-5 mandates. India’s Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP-2020) legally mandates that military platforms prioritize indigenous intellectual property, creating a protected multi-billion-dollar domestic moat.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Mature Silicon — Chapter 1: Market & Legal Moats

nodes.name: Organic Substrate Multi-Die Packaging
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Pragmatic multi-die packaging bypassing expensive silicon interposers. DeepGrid pairs mature 130nm analog/high-voltage dies with sub-28nm digital compute using standard organic laminate substrates, avoiding the million-dollar cost and fragility of silicon interposers.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Mature Silicon — Chapter 6: Block-Level IP Reuse & SiP

nodes.name: 3-Phase Node Roadmap & Arithmetic Check
nodes.description: Technology scaling roadmap from 130/180nm to 28nm with honest ~50-SKU self-audit. DeepGrid’s 3-phase roadmap ships the foundational catalogue on 130/180nm, shrinks logic-bound parts (GNSS baseband, SDR) to 90/55/45nm for channel count, and introduces 28nm for compute in 2030, self-correcting early drafts to a disciplined ~50-SKU Year 5 catalogue.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Semi SKU Compendium — Chapter 14: Node & SKU Roadmap (Sheet 14)

nodes.name: Charlie Munger 14-Point Risk Audit
nodes.communityName: Seed Capital, Financial Model & Charlie Munger Audits
nodes.description: Inversion framework cataloging operational risks and Stop Rules S1–S4. DeepGrid applies Charlie Munger’s inversion mental model to stress-test the company against Chinese price crashes, foundry allocation embargoes, and post-silicon testing delays.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Mature Silicon — Chapter 14: What Could Stop This (Charlie Munger Audit)

nodes.name: ₹10 Cr Financial Model & Use of Funds
nodes.communityName: Seed Capital, Financial Model & Charlie Munger Audits
nodes.description: Seed capital deployment covering 6 MPW runs, ATE lines, and FY31 buildup. The ₹10 Cr ($1.2M) seed round funds 24 months of runway, six parallel MPW factory runs, four full product qualifications, and production mask sets for Chips 1 and 2.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Mature Silicon — Chapter 13: What ₹10 Cr Buys and What It Proves

nodes.name: Hardware DShot RX & Bidirectional Telemetry (dgrid_dshot_rx)
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Hardware DShot receiver + bidirectional telemetry reply engine (slot 0xC in-place extension). Extends slot 0xC in-place with dgrid_dshot_rx and dgrid_dshot_tel, enabling DG32 to operate as a high-performance ESC. Replaces impossible firmware bit-banging that violently collides with the 5 µs FOC loop and eliminates false lockstep divergence trips.
nodes.citation: DG32 Block Spec for Review — dgrid_dshot_rx: DShot receive + bidirectional telemetry reply (13 Sep 2026)

nodes.name: SRAM Architecture: 28 KB vs 32 KB Floorplan Lever
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: OpenFrame 2,900 µm wrapper geometric floorplan trade-off: 3×6 vs 3×7 SRAM macro array. Separates the firmware memory footprint question from the physical floorplan question. Moving from 16 to 14 macros in dual-domain 2DOM reduces the grid from 3×7 to 3×6, deleting an entire macro row and expanding the full-width logic strip from 1.75 mm² to 3.40 mm².
nodes.citation: DG32 Block Spec for Review — §9: SRAM: 28 KB vs 32 KB — separating the two questions

nodes.name: DG32-2DOM Dual-Domain System Architecture (CI2612)
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Dual-clock SoC architecture: 50 MHz lockstep flight-control core + 114 MHz attention engine. The DG32-2DOM (A3) combines the hardened DG32-LITE motor-control core with an INT8 attention engine on a second clock, connected through 4-phase CDC level bridges on a 15.30 mm² die.
nodes.citation: DG32-2DOM System Architecture — Block Definition (chipIgnite CI2612, Sept 2026)

nodes.name: Hardware INT8 Attention Engine & 40-Bit Numerator (dgrid_int8_attn)
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Hardware transformer attention engine with u15 softmax exponential and 40-bit accumulator. Accelerates multi-head self-attention and cross-attention without stalling the CPU domain. Eliminates INT4 quantization collapse by maintaining weights in u15 all the way into a 40-bit signed numerator seat.
nodes.citation: DG32-2DOM System Architecture — Section 4.18: INT8 Attention Engine

nodes.name: AVIP Multimodal Classifier & Stator Current Signature Analysis (CSA)
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Zero-accelerometer bearing fault classifier running in 46.7 ms via on-die phase-current SAR ADC. AVIP detects inner race, outer race, and ball bearing defects using Stator Current Signature Analysis (MCSA). Samples motor current at PWM ripple null to derive mechanical fault frequencies, eliminating external accelerometers.
nodes.citation: DG32-2DOM System Architecture — Section 11: AVIP Bearing-Fault Detection

nodes.name: FOC Control-Loop Budget & Fetch-Bound Headroom
nodes.description: ~100 kHz closed-loop bandwidth: 300 cycles fixed hardware cost, >90% free CPU headroom at 10 kHz. Accounts for every clock cycle in the field-oriented control loop. Offloads ADC sampling (177 cyc) and Park/Clarke transforms (53-58 cyc) to hardware blocks, reserving >90% of execution cycles for firmware observers.
nodes.citation: DG32-2DOM System Architecture — Section 5: Performance and Control-Loop Budget

nodes.name: The $9B Mature-Node Import Funnel & 10x Economics
nodes.description: Dismantling $2M–$5M NRE down to ₹0.6–1.2 Cr across India’s $9B mature-node import market. India imports $23.4B of chips annually, of which $9B is mature-node silicon (≥130 nm). DeepGrid targets 9 addressable chip classes ($0.46B) and cuts development costs by 10× using free open-source EDA and shared MPW runs.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Mature Silicon Whitepaper v3 — Section 1 & 2: What India Buys & Our Costs Line by Line

nodes.name: Chinese Price Crash Stress Test & Stop Rules S1–S4
nodes.communityName: Seed Capital, Financial Model & Charlie Munger Audits
nodes.description: Downside resilience model (FY31 drops to ₹750 Cr) and 4 binding operational stop rules. DeepGrid applies Charlie Munger’s inversion framework to stress-test the company against a catastrophic collapse in Chinese silicon prices. Evaluates revenue resilience and enforces 4 strict, pre-committed operational Stop Rules.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Mature Silicon Whitepaper v3 — Section 12 & 14: Competitor Insulation & Risk Matrix

nodes.name: DGridRiscV Canonical Core Specification
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Standardized RV32IM_Zicsr controller (misa = 0x40001100) shared across 7 of 10 chips. Seven of the ten chips share an identical, parameter-locked RISC-V core generated from VexiiRiscv. Deliberately omits caches, branch prediction, and floating-point to guarantee deterministic sub-1 µs loop latency and bit-exact software verification across foundries.
nodes.citation: DeepGrid Mature Silicon Whitepaper v3 — Section 8: The Processor Every Chip Shares

nodes.name: DG32 64-Pin QFN Physical Pin Map & Packaging
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Standardized 9x9mm 0.5mm-pitch QFN package unifying DG32-LITE (CI2609) and DG32-2DOM (CI2612). Authoritative 64-pin QFN package definition with exact pin assignments across all 4 sides. Guarantees 100% pin-compatible drop-in board replacement between DG32-LITE and DG32-2DOM.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE & DG32-2DOM Preliminary Datasheets — Section 2 & 3: Pinout & Pin Description

nodes.name: DG32 Power Sequencing, Electrical Limits & PCB Layout
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Board design rules: 3.3V-before-1.8V ramp, unused rail ESD biasing, and differential ADC routing. Hardware electrical and PCB layout specifications for DG32 carrier boards. Mandates 3.3V-before-1.8V power sequencing to protect pad rings, unused rail biasing (vdda1/2, vccd2) for ESD steering, and differential microstrip shielding for current sensing.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE & DG32-2DOM Preliminary Datasheets — Section 4, 5 & 9: Electrical Characteristics & Board Guidance

nodes.name: DG32 Standalone Boot ROM & QSPI-XIP Flow
nodes.communityName: Deterministic Motor Control & Lockstep Safety RTL
nodes.description: Autonomous multi-stage bootloader: 115200 8N1 banner, 0xD632_B007 flash detection, and SRAM copy. The DG32 architecture operates without an external management core. At power-on, the baked 64 KB std-cell boot ROM executes autonomously, emits console telemetry, verifies flash header magic 0xD632_B007, copies executable code to SRAM, and jumps to application code.
nodes.citation: DG32-LITE & DG32-2DOM Preliminary Datasheets — Section 6 & 7: Clock, Reset, Boot & Memory Map

DEEPGRID SEMI PVT LTD - PRELIMINARY DATASHEET
DG32-LITE - Preliminary Datasheet
Lockstep RISC-V motor-control SoC on SkyWater sky130A, in a 64-pin QFN. Dual rv32imc cores with a fault
comparator, 32 KB SRAM, 64 KB self-boot ROM and QSPI-XIP, a 3-phase motor peripheral set (PWM, DShot,
encoder, CORDIC, on-die SAR ADC) and UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO. For firmware and hardware/PCB engineers.

Preliminary, pre-silicon. Functional and register detail is from the taped-out RTL and the hardened die. Electrical limits are design
targets and sky130 process nominals pending first-silicon characterisation, and are marked where they are not yet measured. The
flight-control core is frozen until silicon test.
1 Features
• Dual DGridRiscV rv32imc cores in lockstep with a cycle-by-cycle fault comparator and a sticky fault CSR.
• 32 KB on-chip SRAM (no ECC); 64 KB baked boot ROM; QSPI execute-in-place window for external NOR flash.
• 3-phase center-aligned complementary PWM with programmable dead-time and a hardware brake.
• 4-channel DShot ESC engine, pin-muxed onto the PWM output pads.
• Quadrature + Hall encoder with edge timestamps; CORDIC (sin/cos, atan2, magnitude) for field-oriented control.
• On-die 8-bit differential SAR ADC for phase-current feedback, PWM-triggered.
• Two UARTs, an SPI master, a 7-bit I2C master, 14-pin GPIO, two timers, a windowed watchdog and rail supervisor.
• Interrupt controller; standalone self-boot (no management core); SLVERR on any unmapped access.
• Single 50 MHz clock domain; whole die powered from a 1.8 V rail; 3.3 V I/O.

6 Clock, reset and boot
6.1 Clock and reset
A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs
are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be
used, pull the unused one high. The DG32-LITE die runs entirely from this one 50 MHz domain.
6.2 Boot flow
The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help:
• Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz).
• Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length).
• Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2).
• Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM.
• A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are
reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM
first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

9 Board design guidance (hardware / PCB)
• Motor half-bridge gate driver on PWM_AH..CL (pins 3-8); the outputs are complementary with programmable
dead-time. Respect the driver's shoot-through spec; the die also has a hardware brake that forces all six low.
• Route PWM_TRIG (pin 11) to nothing external unless you want the ADC-sample instant on a test point; it fires at the
centre-aligned current-ripple null.
• Wire the encoder A/B/Z (pins 12-14) and Hall A/B/C (pins 15,16,22) directly; inputs are 2-flop synchronised and 3.3 V.
• SAR ADC inputs ADC_VINP (62) and ADC_VINN (2) are differential, 0 to 1.8 V - scale phase-current shunt amplifiers
into that window and keep the pair matched and short.
• QSPI NOR boot flash on pins 32-37 (add CSN1=41 for a second device / PSRAM); a 3.3 V W25Q / S25FL works.
Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor.
• I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V).
• Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry.
• FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor
for a hardware trip.
• Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad
from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers.
JTAG idles safely with no probe. TMS (pin 25) and TDI (pin 26) are weakly pulled up on die, TCK (pin 24) weakly pulled down, so
an unconnected JTAG header will not disturb the part.

path and motor peripheral set; adds a memory-mapped attention engine (0xE000_0000) that runs on clk_fast_i and
reaches memory through clock-domain-crossing bridges. For firmware and hardware/PCB engineers.

Preliminary, pre-silicon. Functional and register detail is from the taped-out RTL and the hardened die. Electrical limits are design
targets and sky130 process nominals pending first-silicon characterisation, and are marked where they are not yet measured. The
flight-control core is frozen until silicon test.
1 Features
• Everything in DG32-LITE: dual rv32imc lockstep core, 32 KB SRAM, 64 KB boot ROM, QSPI-XIP, and the full motor
peripheral set (PWM, DShot, encoder, CORDIC, SAR ADC) plus UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO.
• INT8 attention accelerator (0xE000_0000): one kick computes a band of query rows of one head end to end (QK^T,
softmax/EXP, E.V, requantise to int8), bit-exact to the golden model.
• Attention datapath: shared LANES-wide MAC array, 256-entry u15 EXP table, 40-bit numerator (exact to NK=131072),
one reciprocal per row; ~3242 cycles/row analytic at LANES=16.
• Second clock domain: the engine runs on clk_fast_i (114 MHz) and crosses to the 50 MHz CPU domain through 2-flop
CDC bridges, so it never stalls the frozen control core.
• Own die (3400 x 4500 um) with the attention K/V buffers on sky130 SRAM macros next to the SAR analog corner.

6 Clock, reset and boot
6.1 Clock and reset
A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs
are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be
used, pull the unused one high. DG32-2DOM adds a second clock, clk_fast_i (114 MHz), for the attention engine; the CPU
and all peripherals stay in the 50 MHz domain and the two are bridged by CDC logic.
6.2 Boot flow
The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help:
• Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz).
• Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length).
• Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2).
• Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM.
• A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are
reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM
first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

9 Board design guidance (hardware / PCB)
• Motor half-bridge gate driver on PWM_AH..CL (pins 3-8); the outputs are complementary with programmable
dead-time. Respect the driver's shoot-through spec; the die also has a hardware brake that forces all six low.
• Route PWM_TRIG (pin 11) to nothing external unless you want the ADC-sample instant on a test point; it fires at the
centre-aligned current-ripple null.
• Wire the encoder A/B/Z (pins 12-14) and Hall A/B/C (pins 15,16,22) directly; inputs are 2-flop synchronised and 3.3 V.
• SAR ADC inputs ADC_VINP (62) and ADC_VINN (2) are differential, 0 to 1.8 V - scale phase-current shunt amplifiers
into that window and keep the pair matched and short.
• QSPI NOR boot flash on pins 32-37 (add CSN1=41 for a second device / PSRAM); a 3.3 V W25Q / S25FL works.
Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor.
• I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V).
• Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry.
• FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor
for a hardware trip.
• Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad
from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers.
• The attention engine adds no board signals; budget for clk_fast_i only if the CI2612 die brings it out to a pad rather
than deriving it on-die.

reaches memory through clock-domain-crossing bridges. For firmware and hardware/PCB engineers.

Preliminary, pre-silicon. Functional and register detail is from the taped-out RTL and the hardened die. Electrical limits are design
targets and sky130 process nominals pending first-silicon characterisation, and are marked where they are not yet measured. The
flight-control core is frozen until silicon test.
1 Features
• Everything in DG32-LITE: dual rv32imc lockstep core, 32 KB SRAM, 64 KB boot ROM, QSPI-XIP, and the full motor
peripheral set (PWM, DShot, encoder, CORDIC, SAR ADC) plus UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO.
• INT8 attention accelerator (0xE000_0000): one kick computes a band of query rows of one head end to end (QK^T,
softmax/EXP, E.V, requantise to int8), bit-exact to the golden model.
• Attention datapath: shared LANES-wide MAC array, 256-entry u15 EXP table, 40-bit numerator (exact to NK=131072),
one reciprocal per row; ~3242 cycles/row analytic at LANES=16.
• Second clock domain: the engine runs on clk_fast_i (114 MHz) and crosses to the 50 MHz CPU domain through 2-flop
CDC bridges, so it never stalls the frozen control core.
• Own die (3400 x 4500 um) with the attention K/V buffers on sky130 SRAM macros next to the SAR analog corner.

6 Clock, reset and boot
6.1 Clock and reset
A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs
are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be
used, pull the unused one high. DG32-2DOM adds a second clock, clk_fast_i (114 MHz), for the attention engine; the CPU
and all peripherals stay in the 50 MHz domain and the two are bridged by CDC logic.
6.2 Boot flow
The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help:
• Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz).
• Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length).
• Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2).
• Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM.
• A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are
reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM
first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

9 Board design guidance (hardware / PCB)
• Motor half-bridge gate driver on PWM_AH..CL (pins 3-8); the outputs are complementary with programmable
dead-time. Respect the driver's shoot-through spec; the die also has a hardware brake that forces all six low.
• Route PWM_TRIG (pin 11) to nothing external unless you want the ADC-sample instant on a test point; it fires at the
centre-aligned current-ripple null.
• Wire the encoder A/B/Z (pins 12-14) and Hall A/B/C (pins 15,16,22) directly; inputs are 2-flop synchronised and 3.3 V.
• SAR ADC inputs ADC_VINP (62) and ADC_VINN (2) are differential, 0 to 1.8 V - scale phase-current shunt amplifiers
into that window and keep the pair matched and short.
• QSPI NOR boot flash on pins 32-37 (add CSN1=41 for a second device / PSRAM); a 3.3 V W25Q / S25FL works.
Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor.
• I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V).
• Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry.
• FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor
for a hardware trip.
• Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad
from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers.
• The attention engine adds no board signals; budget for clk_fast_i only if the CI2612 die brings it out to a pad rather
than deriving it on-die.

survives it, which keeps the OpenFrame-correct non-volatile boot path intact. Deepening it from 4 KB to 16 KB was
measured as effectively free.
Why standalone matters. OpenFrame has nothing else to start the chip. The boot ROM runs the UART banner, reads the
flash header (magic 0xD632_B007) through the 0x1 window, copies the image into SRAM, and jumps to it - all with no
management core.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the private boot ROM alone; the 0x1 XIP window and
SRAM are reachable by loads and stores, not by fetch. Code does not execute in place from external NOR - it is copied to
SRAM first and run from there.

11 Application: AVIP bearing-fault detection
The DG32-2DOM attention engine exists to run models like AVIP, an INT8 bearing-fault classifier (dgrid-a8w8). AVIP is
multimodal - a time branch and an FFT branch, each a small conv stack plus a gated recurrent cell - fused by two
self-attention blocks and one cross-attention block, ending in a per-class head. Those attention blocks are exactly what the
engine accelerates. The shipped CWRU-trained model is 47,076 parameters at 94-95% held-out-load accuracy with INT8
equal to FP32; the full AVIP topology is 478,277 parameters. Both map onto the same op set with no new RTL.

Where a scalar core is strong
The absence of a MAC array reverses the usual ranking. Comparisons and table lookups cost almost nothing here.
Tree ensembles are the best accuracy per cycle on this part
A 100-tree random forest at depth 8 is roughly 800 comparisons and no
multiplies at all — 0.06 ms, supporting rates above 1 kHz. A neural network
of comparable accuracy on bearing-fault or power-quality classification costs
50–500× more cycles.
This is not a compromise made for the hardware. On the CWRU bearing
benchmark a random forest over five time-domain features reaches 95.6 %,
and cutting from nine features to five costs 0.1 %. A review of 42 papers
finds SVM at 95–100 % against deep methods at 97–100 % — statistically
indistinguishable.
Model capacity is not the bottleneck on these tasks. Signal
conditioning is.
The ordering that follows
First choice — tree ensembles, linear discriminants, PCA with Hotelling T²,
Mahalanobis distance. Sub-millisecond, kHz-capable, inspectable in the field.
Second choice — small dense networks and autoencoders, where a
nonlinear boundary genuinely earns its place. Still sub-millisecond.
Reach for last — recurrent and convolutional models. A GRU at 2.95 ms and
a 1D-CNN at 10.3 ms both fit, but only where the raw waveform carries
something hand-built features miss.
Design rule. Spend effort on band selection, envelope demodulation and
operating-condition normalisation before spending it on model capacity.

Why this matters more than the model
A published feature-ranking study across twelve features found demodulated
features evaluated at the known fault frequency outrank raw statistical
moments by a factor of 4–5. Hilbert-Huang amplitude at the outer-race
frequency scored 225.9; peak-to-peak scored 51.8.
That is the whole argument for spending cycles on envelope demodulation
and band selection rather than on a larger classifier. The envelope chain is
also cheap: band-pass, rectify, low-pass, decimate to 1–2 kS/s, then a modest
FFT. Do the decimation before buffering and the working set never exceeds a
few kB.

What the sensing supports
Compute is not the binding constraint on these thirty use cases. The analog front end is.
The current-based use cases need more than 8 bits
ISO 13373-2 gives usable dynamic range as D = 6(N−1) dB, so eight bits yields 42 dB. ISO 20958 states rotor-bar sidebands sit 100 to
1,000 times below the fundamental — −40 to −60 dBc. The entire diagnostic range sits at or below the quantisation floor. Broken rotor bar,
eccentricity and inter-turn short detection need either analog fundamental suppression and gain ahead of the converter, or 12–16 bits.
A second constraint compounds it. Sideband separation is 2·s·f₁ — roughly 3 Hz at full load, 0.5 Hz at light load — so these use cases need
30–100 second records at stable load and speed with 0.01–0.05 Hz resolution. A 2²⁰-point FFT is 8 MB and does not fit. Use Goertzel
evaluated at the predicted sideband frequencies, which is why the electrical use cases on slide 06 are costed that way and not with an FFT.
Tier 1 — one accelerometer
The highest-value addition. Bearings are 44 % of
motor failures and are the weakest fault class
for current-only sensing; rotor bars, where
current is strongest, are 8–10 %. Needs ≥5 kHz
usable bandwidth — many low-cost MEMS
parts roll off at 1–3 kHz, below the bearing
resonance band, which makes envelope analysis
useless. Mounting matters as much as the part:
stud mounting per ISO 13373-1, not magnet or
adhesive.
Tier 2 — three-phase current and voltage
Unlocks negative-sequence detection of stator
inter-turn shorts, instantaneous power signature
analysis and Park's vector per ISO 20958 Annex
A. Needs a multi-channel converter; the part
currently has one differential channel.

1 Features
• Dual DGridRiscV rv32imc cores in lockstep with a cycle-by-cycle fault comparator and a sticky fault CSR.
• 32 KB on-chip SRAM (no ECC); 64 KB baked boot ROM; QSPI execute-in-place window for external NOR flash.
• 3-phase center-aligned complementary PWM with programmable dead-time and a hardware brake.
• 4-channel DShot ESC engine, pin-muxed onto the PWM output pads.
• Quadrature + Hall encoder with edge timestamps; CORDIC (sin/cos, atan2, magnitude) for field-oriented control.
• On-die 8-bit differential SAR ADC for phase-current feedback, PWM-triggered.
• Two UARTs, an SPI master, a 7-bit I2C master, 14-pin GPIO, two timers, a windowed watchdog and rail supervisor.
• Interrupt controller; standalone self-boot (no management core); SLVERR on any unmapped access.
• Single 50 MHz clock domain; whole die powered from a 1.8 V rail; 3.3 V I/O.

6 Clock, reset and boot
6.1 Clock and reset
A single core clock enters on CLK (pin 31), 3.3 V CMOS, 50 MHz design target. There is no on-die PLL. Two reset inputs
are ANDed on die: the OpenFrame harness resetb (pin 21, active low) and RST_N (pin 28, active low); either may be
used, pull the unused one high. The DG32-LITE die runs entirely from this one 50 MHz domain.
6.2 Boot flow
The die is standalone - no management core. At power-on the on-die 64 KB boot ROM runs with no external help:
• Emit the boot banner on UART0 (pin 42) at 115200 8N1 (baud divider fixed for 50 MHz).
• Read the QSPI NOR flash header through the 0x1 window (boot magic 0xD632_B007, then length).
• Copy the flash image into SRAM over the QSPI quad-output-fast-read (0x6B, 1-1-4, 8 dummy cycles, SCLK = clk/2).
• Jump to the copied image and run from SRAM/ROM.
• A UART monitor (r/w/j/i commands) is available if the flash is blank, so a bare board is still inspectable.
Instruction fetch is ROM-only. The CPU fetch bus is wired to the boot ROM alone. The QSPI-XIP window and SRAM are
reachable by loads and stores, not by instruction fetch - code does not execute in place from external NOR, it is copied to SRAM
first. Firmware and linker scripts must place executable code in SRAM.

9 Board design guidance (hardware / PCB)
• Motor half-bridge gate driver on PWM_AH..CL (pins 3-8); the outputs are complementary with programmable
dead-time. Respect the driver's shoot-through spec; the die also has a hardware brake that forces all six low.
• Route PWM_TRIG (pin 11) to nothing external unless you want the ADC-sample instant on a test point; it fires at the
centre-aligned current-ripple null.
• Wire the encoder A/B/Z (pins 12-14) and Hall A/B/C (pins 15,16,22) directly; inputs are 2-flop synchronised and 3.3 V.
• SAR ADC inputs ADC_VINP (62) and ADC_VINN (2) are differential, 0 to 1.8 V - scale phase-current shunt amplifiers
into that window and keep the pair matched and short.
• QSPI NOR boot flash on pins 32-37 (add CSN1=41 for a second device / PSRAM); a 3.3 V W25Q / S25FL works.
Without a flash the ROM drops to the UART monitor.
• I2C_SCL (53) and I2C_SDA (54) are open-drain - the carrier must supply the pull-ups (typ 2.2-4.7 k to 3.3 V).
• Bring UART0 (42/43) to a USB-UART for the boot banner and console; UART1 (44/45) is free for telemetry.
• FAULT_N (59) is an active-low fault output from the lockstep/supervisor - route it to the driver enable or a supervisor
for a hardware trip.
• Provide 3.3 V and 1.8 V per Section 5; the 100 production parts need a carrier with the 64-pin QFN footprint (KiCad
from chipfoundry/caravel_board), gate drives, encoder, an optional external SPI ADC, and UART/JTAG headers.
JTAG idles safely with no probe. TMS (pin 25) and TDI (pin 26) are weakly pulled up on die, TCK (pin 24) weakly pulled down, so
an unconnected JTAG header will not disturb the part.

1. Why firmware cannot do this (confirming Ayaz's argument)
DShot600 is 1.67 µs/bit; the 0/1 decision is a high-time of 625 ns vs 1250 ns. At 50 MHz that is
31 vs 62 cycles, so the decode needs ~±15-cycle (±300 ns) edge placement — achievable only
by a busy-wait loop with interrupts off for

the lockstep compare window — dgrid_lockstep_check  compares every committed
store; a firmware bit-bang that branches on pad reads produces store streams whose
timing depends on an asynchronous input, which is exactly the class of behaviour the
checker is designed to flag.
And bidirectional reply is impossible in firmware regardless of speed: the ESC must turn
the pad from input to output ~30 µs after the command frame ends and drive a 21-bit reply —
the pad has no output-enable today. This is a pad-ring fact, not a software one.
Conclusion: hardware RX + hardware reply, or no ESC role.
2. What exists today (baseline)
dgrid_dshot  (slot 0xC, rtl/dgrid_dshot.sv ) is transmit-only: 4 channels, one shared bit-time
counter, per-channel 16-bit frame + CRC4, programmable BITPERIOD / T0H / T1H . Its only pins
are output [3:0] dshot_o . The four channels reach the pads only through SYSCTL PINMUX[0] ,
which AND-ORs them onto the PWM high-side pads AH / BH / CH / SAMPLE_TRIG
( dg32_lite_top.sv:775-792 ). The low-side PWM pads are never muxed, so a mis-set mux cannot
shoot through a bridge.
Pad budget is 44/44 with zero spare. There is no pad for a receiver. The RX path therefore
must reuse the same four pads, which means those pads become bidirectional. That is the
single most consequential change in this spec (§7).
3. Protocol facts the design depends on
3.1 Command frame (FC → ESC), what RX decodes
16 bits, MSB first: [15:5]  throttle (11 b) · [4]  telemetry request · [3:0]  CRC4. Each bit is one
pulse of fixed period; high-time encodes the value (long = 1, short = 0).

3.3 Telemetry reply (ESC → FC), what the reply engine sends
The reply is not a DShot command frame, so it cannot reuse the TX engine's shifter
unmodified:
1. Payload: 16 bits = [15:4]  eRPM period (3-bit exponent e , 9-bit mantissa m ; period_µs = m
<< e ) · [3:0]  CRC where crc = ~(v ^ v>>4 ^ v>>8) & 0xF  over the 12-bit period field.
2. GCR 4b→5b encode each nibble (table: 19 1B 12 13 1D 15 16 17 1A 09 0A 0B 1E 0D 0E 0F )
→ 20 bits.
3. Transition-encode to 21 bits: out[0] = 0; out[i] = out[i-1] ^ G[i-1]  — a 1  in the GCR
stream is a level transition, not a level.
4. Transmit inverted, at 5/4 the command bit rate (DShot600 → 750 kbit/s, 1.33 µs/bit =
66.7 cycles), starting ~30 µs after the command frame's last edge.
The FC decodes edges back with G = s ^ (s >> 1) . This is the Betaflight/Bluejay/AM32
convention; get any of the three steps wrong and every FC on the market reports CRC errors.
4. Architecture
Recommendation: extend slot 0xC in place, not a new slot. The RX and reply engines are
added inside dgrid_dshot  as two self-contained sub-modules ( dgrid_dshot_rx , dgrid_dshot_tel ),
sharing the existing AXI slave, the pad mux and the bit-timing registers. Reasons: (a) the
address map has no free slot without touching the decoder and error-slave logic that is frozen for
tape-in; (b) RX and TX are mutually exclusive on the same pads, so one owner of the pad
direction is safer than two; (c) BITPERIOD/T0H/T1H  already encode the speed class — RX derives
its threshold from them by default.
                       ┌───────────── dgrid_dshot (slot 0xC) ─────────────┐
   AXI-lite ──────────►│ regs │ TX engine (existing) ───────────┐          │
                       │      │                                  │ mux/dir │──► pad_o[3:0]
                       │      │ dgrid_d

Synchroniser + filter add a fixed 3-cycle (60 ns) latency to both edges, so measured width
is unaffected.
4.2 Reply engine dgrid_dshot_tel  (per channel)
Armed when TELEM_EN=1  and a valid frame with telem=1  arrives (or TELEM_ALWAYS=1  —
bidirectional FCs expect a reply on every frame).
Waits TURNAROUND  cycles from the command frame's last edge, then asserts pad_oe , drives
the 21-bit stream from TELEMn  at TELEMPERIOD  cycles/bit (inverted), then releases pad_oe
and returns the pad to input.
GCR + transition encoding (§3.3) done in hardware from the 12-bit period value firmware
writes to TELEMn . Firmware supplies only {e, m} ; CRC, GCR and transition coding are
hardware. This keeps the firmware side to one register write per commutation-period
update.
If a new command frame's first edge arrives while a reply is being driven, the reply is
aborted and OE released within one cycle — never fight the FC for the wire. TEL_ABORT
status bit is set.
4.3 Direction ownership
pad_oe  per channel is the OR of: TX engine BUSY  (existing TX role, always drives) and
dgrid_dshot_tel  driving . In RX-only or RX+reply roles the TX engine is never started, so the pad
idles as input. PINMUX[0]  continues to select DShot vs PWM; PWM-role pads remain output-
only (OE forced high) so the bridge-safety property is preserved.

Reset state: RX_EN=0 , all thresholds 0 (→ derived defaults), all pads input-disabled only if the
wrapper's pad config leaves them so — see §7.
Note on clearing VALID : W1C is the safe default and matches the other DG32 peripherals.
Read-to-clear is not recommended: the lockstep checker mirrors bus reads to the CHECKER core
two cycles late, so a read with a side-effect would be observed by both cores but the side-effect
happens once — safe in practice, but it is exactly the kind of subtlety the design avoids
elsewhere. Keep W1C.

6. Interrupts
One new source into dgrid_irq  (0xDF): dshot_rx_irq = (IRQ_FRAME_EN & |VALID) | (IRQ_ERR_EN &
|(CRC_ERR|OVERRUN|TEL_ABORT)) . Level, cleared by W1C of the underlying flags. dgrid_irq  has a
16-bit raw vector with bits 0–6 and 8 (attention, 2dom) used; bit 7 is 1'b0  today and is the
natural slot ( rtl/dgrid_irq.sv:58 ). Bits 9–15 are also free. Follow the existing convention: add
dshot_rx_i = 1'b0  as a defaulted port so the frozen lite netlist is unchanged when the port is left
unconnected — and tie it explicitly in the top (sv2v drops port defaults).
7. Pad-ring change — the real cost of this feature
The four DShot pads are io[26] P_PWM_AH , io[28] P_PWM_BH , io[30] P_PWM_CH , io[32] P_PWM_TRIG
( openframe/openframe_project_wrapper.v:134-136 ). Today they are class PC_OUT  ( pad_class()  at
line 470: i >= P_PWM_AH && i <= P_PWM_TRIG ), i.e. gpio_dm = 110 , gpio_inp_dis = 1 , oeb  tied to
constant drive (lines 408–414).
The wrapper already has the class we need: PC_BIDIR  ( gpio_dm = 110 , gpio_inp_dis = 0 , oeb
dynamic) is what QSPI IO0–3, I²C and the three GPIOs use. So the change is three edits, not a
new pad mode:

Why it still carries risk: the whole per-pad config table rests on an item your tape-in notes
flag — the exact gpio_dm  / inp_dis  enc

out of reset. pad_oe  must follow: input during rst_n_i  low, so a resetting DG32 never drives a

during reset. AL/BL/CL  are unchanged.
8. Timing, cost and verification
Edge precision at 50 MHz (20 ns/cycle): the decision margin is T1H − T0H . DShot300: 63
cycles (±630 ns) — trivial. DShot600: 31 cycles (±310 ns) — comfortable. DShot1200: 15
cycles (±150 ns) — works on paper, but the synchroniser's ±1-cycle sampling jitter plus FC-
side jitter eats a third of it. Recommend DShot600 as the supported maximum;
DShot1200 best-effort.
Area estimate: per channel — 12-bit width counter, 16-bit RX shifter, 4-bit CRC, RX FSM (~70
flops); 21-bit reply shifter, 12-bit period counter, GCR/transition encoder (~50 flops); status/flags
(~8). ×4 ≈ ~520 flops plus shared registers (~100) and 8 synchroniser flops. Roughly 1,500–
2,500 std cells — about 3–5% of the lite die's 50,550. Consistent with Ayaz's "cheap": the TX
engine closes at 172.9 MHz against 50 MHz, and RX has no deeper logic.
Verification plan (before integration, all standalone): 1. tb_dshot_rx  — loopback: existing
TX engine drives RX through a modelled pad at all four speeds; every throttle 0–2047 × telem
0/1; assert RXFRAME == transmitted  and VALID . Also inject each single-bit corruption → assert
CRC_ERR , never VALID . 2. Glitch/desync: inject a 40 ns glitch mid-frame; assert timeout resync
and that the next frame decodes clean. 3. Overrun: two frames back-to-back without a read →
OVERRUN . 4. tb_dshot_tel  — reply stream captured by a reference FC decoder implementing G
= s ^ (s>>1)  + GCR table + CRC check, written independently

Both can be true. The question is whether 2dom can fit at 2,900 µm with 32 KB, and the codex
branch is already answering it empirically: 2dom/13  is a keep-32 KB spread-floorplan test,
2dom/12  a 24 KB variant. If 13  routes and closes, keep 32 KB and drop the 28 KB idea. If
only the reduced-SRAM variants fit, then the firmware team gets 28 KB and the 2 KB
reusable buffer stops being optional. Decide from those two runs, not from either side's
estimate. Note the lite die is unaffected either way — it stays 32 KB.

RTL 1. rtl/dgrid_dshot_rx.sv  — per-channel RX decoder (§4.1), 4 instances, parameterised on
TW=12 . 2. rtl/dgrid_dshot_tel.sv  — per-channel GCR/transition reply engine (§4.2). 3. Extend
dgrid_dshot.sv : registers 0x24–0x5C (§5), pad_i[3:0]  input, pad_oe[3:0]  output, irq_o ,
direction FSM (§4.3). Existing 0x00–0x20 behaviour and the TX engine unchanged; tb_dshot
must still pass bit-identical. 4. dg32_lite_top.sv : route pad_i / pad_oe  for the four muxed pads;

In plain words: the chips India buys from abroad, why we can make them here —
and now, chip by chip, who buys each one, what it earns, and the rules that guard the money.
India buys almost every one of its simpler chips from other countries. About $9 billion of them
a year. These are the unexciting parts inside every vehicle, electricity meter, drone and defence
box: power chips, small processors, motor drivers, data-line chips, voltage monitors.
Nobody in India makes them. The reason is not skill. It is that designing a chip the normal
way costs $2 to $5 million before you sell one unit, and these chips sell in small numbers. This
document explains how we cut that cost by about ten times, what we have already built, what
₹10 Cr would buy — and, new in this edition, the money one chip at a time, the named anchor
customers, and the stop rules we set for ourselves in advance.

1 What India buys, and why nobody here makes it
Start with one number. Last year India imported $23.4 billion of chips. That figure is from UN

meter front ends. These are not exciting chips. But they are most of the chips in any product. A
car has one or two advanced processors and several dozen of these older ones. A smart electricity

• software licences for design tools: $0.5–1 million every year
• a full set of photographic masks to print the chip: $0.5–1 million

PART THREE
The machine: this process, this loop, this library 130 nm is the right process for these chips for
reasons of physics, not price. The loop that turns that into a range of products runs every 198
days. And what builds up over time is not the chips. It is the library underneath them.
4 Why 130 nm is the right process, not the cheap one
In chips, people assume newer is better. For this kind of chip that is simply wrong, and the reasons
are physical. High voltage works here. 130 nm and 180 nm factory processes offer thick-oxide
transistors and LDMOS devices. These handle 5 volts up to 120 volts directly. So a 28 V aircraft
power rail, a 120 V motor supply and a 0.9 V digital core can all sit on one chip. On a newer,
smaller process the power circuits move back onto the circuit board as separate parts. That is the
opposite of what you want. More board space, more parts to buy, more things to fail. This is why
four of our ten chips exist at all. Chip 1 has a 5–120 V converter next to a 200 MHz processor.
Chip 3 puts an aircraft-standard input stage, an LDMOS power stage and four power rails on one
chip. Chip 5 needs a 5 V-tolerant output ring. Chip 8 drives 0–12 V into a display panel across
3,840 outputs. None of these can be made on a newer process at any price. Radiation resistance
comes from size. A cosmic ray can flip a stored bit. The bigger the transistor, the more charge
is needed to flip it, so bigger transistors are harder to disturb. Protection methods such as DICE
latches and triple redundancy cost chip area, and area is the one thing an older process has spare.
On chip 3 the power sequencer uses triple redundancy and DICE latches, and this costs a f

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
from a temperature-corrected reference circuit and closely matched resistors. For chip 5 the argu-
ment reverses completely. A newer process is actively worse for a line driver. A line driver needs
a 5 V-tolerant thick output ring with strong static-discharge protection. Newer processes do not
have one. This is why interface chips from every major company are still made on older processes
today. One place the process is a hard limit. Chip 7 is a 4D radar front end. It cannot be built on
ordinary CMOS. The sky130 process will not reach 77 GHz. Not slowly, not expensively. Not at
all. The IHP SG13G2 process is a 130 nm SiGe process with special high-speed transistors that
reach about 350 GHz. This is the transistor type that real 77 GHz car radar uses. So the design
splits into two chips, one on each process, with the boundary at the analogue-to-digital converter.
One result of this belongs here and not in a footnote. You cannot prototype a 77 GHz front end on
an FPGA. FPGA testing covers the digital half only. The high-frequency half is proven in silicon
or not at all. AND ONE PLACE WHERE A FREE DESIGN KIT IS A PROBLEM, NOT A
BENEFIT Everything above is true of the factory process. It is not yet true of the parts library. A
paid 130 nm design kit comes with a tested library of analogue building blocks: reference circuits,
protection cells rated to a stated level, memory. A free kit does not. So the ±15 kV protection
ring on chip 5, the temperature-stable reference on chip 3 and the memory on chip 1 are targets
with no tested example to copy. We have to build and prove each one in silicon before it becomes
a datasheet number. That is real work and real schedule. It is

6.1 What a shared die can and cannot do
TinyTapeout puts hundreds of small designs on one die behind a shared wrapper. Each design
gets a fixed tile of space, and a switch picks which one connects to the shared pins. Only one
design works at a time. That is excellent for what it does, and completely unable to do four
things:
• Space. A tile is about 0.02 mm². That is a few hundred to a few thousand logic gates. A motor
controller
with a power converter, a 16-bit converter, seven output channels and a processor is several mm².
No sellable chip fits in a tile.
• Analogue and high voltage. The wrapper is digital only. No high-voltage devices, no reference
circuits,
no converters, no thick output ring, no high-speed radar transistors. Chips 3, 5, 6, 7 and the
output stage of chip 8 cannot be tested this way at all.
• Using many pins at once. The pins are shared and time-switched. You cannot test 3,840 display
out-
puts, or seven motor channels, or four radar receivers. You can show a digital block works. You
cannot measure noise, power supply rejection, or accuracy across temperature from a tile.
• Datasheet measurements.
6.2 The change of word
The mistake is calling a tile a chip. It is not. It is a building block. And every chip in our range
breaks down into digital building blocks, and those do fit in a tile: the motor control datapath,
the tuning loop, the meter filter, the fault table, the noise filters, the lockstep comparator, the
display timing generator, the network shaper, the encryption cores, the memory controller, the
radar processing control. Do not say “1,000 chips in five years.” A chip means a datasheet, an
approval, a test program and a place on an appr

6.5 Two things we would argue with in our own plan
Custom chip-to-chip connections stop us selling a single die. We chose not to use the UCIe industry
standard. That avoids a real area and power cost, but it means no other company can buy one of
our dies as a component. If selling dies is ever the plan, the connection standard has to be chosen
now. Changing it later is a redesign. Packaging is a supply chain that is not yet in our plan. The
end goal is six chips in one package: power,
motor drive, communications, safety, control and analogue, with the 28 nm AI chip joining later.
This multiplies volume, because one packaged product contains six chips. But it needs an assembly
partner, package-level testing, and an answer to what happens when one chip in six is faulty.
That last question forces you to test every chip before assembly, and §10 carries it as a cost and a
schedule line rather than a detail. One method, one library. The next question is which factories
it runs in, and whether ”works on any process” survives contact with an analogue circuit.

8.1 Every missing feature is a decision
A reviewer will read the second half of that table as a list of gaps unless we explain each one.
No caches.
A cache is a small fast memory that keeps recently used data.
It usually helps,
but sometimes it misses and then the access takes far longer. These are control chips that must
respond in a guaranteed time. A cache turns a guaranteed worst case into an average, and that
is the wrong trade for a motor loop, a power sequencer or a safety monitor. Our processor goes
straight to closely attached memory with a fixed access time. Chip 1’s hardware control loop
responds in under 1 microsecond, and that number only means something because nothing in the
path can miss. No branch prediction. Same reason, plus chip area. A cost you always pay is easier
to plan for than one you usually avoid. And these control loops are short and dominated by data
processing rather than branching. No floating-point unit. Every calculation in our range uses
fixed-point maths by design. Fixed-point is smaller, faster, and gives exactly the same answer on
every chip. That matters when the same calculation must match between a screened chip and a
commercial one. Our floating-point work at 130 nm sits on the test chip as a separate engine, not
inside the control processor. No compressed instructions. Compressed instructions save memory
space. That matters when instruction memory is off the chip and expensive. Here it is on the chip
and sized to the job, and removing the feature removes an alignment case from the fetch path.
Memory protection instead of a full memory manager. These chips run bare-metal code or a small
realtime operating system. What they ne

9.1 Chip 1 · BLDC motor controller
What it is. A DGridRiscV processor at 200 MHz. A hardware control loop that responds in
under 1 microsecond. A full motor-control calculation unit. Seven output channels for driving the
motor. A 16-bit converter to read sensors. A 5–120 V power converter. And 256 KB to 1 MB of
memory that keeps its contents without power.

What it replaces. Today a customer buys two chips: a driver chip such as a DRV83xx, plus a
separate microcontroller, plus the components between them. We put all of it on one chip. The

That is a direct match, though the listing is for the whole motor unit and not the chip inside it.

Anchor customer, named: Airgap Technology — an Indian maker of electric-vehicle motors

9.2 Chip 2 · Smart-meter chip
What it is. A six-channel measurement front end accurate to 24 bits, with a filter chain that
averages 256 samples. It calculates real,

What it replaces. A measurement chip such as an ADE9153 or V9203, plus a separate meter
microcontroller. We combine them behind one internal communication network. Why this pro-
cess. A 24-bit measurement circuit needs accurate resistors, good capacitors and closely matched
transistors. 130 nm has all three. Where it sells, and how many. India’s national programme to
install about 250 million smart meters. We estimate 10 to 30 million units a year at peak, at $2
to $5 each. The legal or demand hook. Tamper detection is a requirement in meter tenders, not
an optional feature. That makes it something the chip must do, not something software can add
later. Status. The blocks are tested on FPGA. The product is a 130 nm chip at 200 MHz. Because
a free design kit has no built-in flash memory, we use read-only memory plus error-corrected RAM
plus encrypted external memory. A version using SCL’s memory is planned for sealed meters.
First factory run: cycle 1, alongside chip 1.
9.3 Chip 3 · High-reliability power chip
What it is.
An input stage that meets the DO-160 and MIL-STD-461 aircraft standards.
A
first-stage converter with a stable control loop. Four power outputs that switch on in a controlled
order and limit their own current. A temperature-stable voltage reference accurate to 12 parts
per million per degree. A converter for reading telemetry. And a control state machine protected
against cosmic-ray upsets using DICE latches and triple redundancy.

What it replaces. Texas Instruments and Analog Devices military-grade power chips inside aircraft
and armoured-vehicle boxes. This is genuine analogue design — a voltage reference, a compensated
control loop, a telemetry converter — not a digital chip with a power stage bolted on. Why this
process. High-voltage devices let a 28 V input stage and a 0.9 V processor supply sit on one
chip. And radiation resistance comes from the transistor size itself, not from something added on.
Where it sells, and how many. We estimate 10,000 to 50,000 units a year in Indian high-reliability
power, at $50 to $200 each once screened. Small volume, 60–75 % gross margin, and once approved
it stays on the vendor list for decades. The legal or demand hook. SRIJAN category NSG-5962.
PIL-5 lists two tank power converters from BEL, 16–40 V input at 4 A, due December 2026 and
December 2028. Status. MIL-883 screening process. Radiation protection by design only. We
make no radiation-hardened claim beyond that.
9.4 Chip 4 · Lockstep microcontroller
What it is. Two DGridRiscV processors running the same program two clock cycles apart. If they
ever disagree, comparators on the bus and at the output raise a fault signal within two cycles.
Error correction is carried on every internal connection.

not speed. An older process makes that duplication affordable, and makes the radiation protection

What it is. Thick-oxide 5 V output stages. Receivers with 30 millivolts of noise margin. A fail-safe

What it replaces. Interface chips from Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Renesas. Two
things drive this: the original part gets discontinued, and defence buyers face sourcing rules that
block the import. Why this process. A newer process is actively worse for this kind of chip. A
line driver needs a 5 V-tolerant thick output ring, and newer processes do not have one. Where
it sells, and how many. We estimate 20 to 60 million units a year, because one transceiver ships
with every node on every communication bus. $0.4 to $1.5 commercially, and 10 to 100 times
that for screened versions.
The legal or demand hook.
Replacing a discontinued part is the
fastest conversation available with a defence company, because the part is already approved into a
system that can no longer buy it. What they need is an exact electrical match, not a new design
win. Status. Signal timing, not raw data rate, decides how many nodes and how long a cable
can be, and the design is budgeted for that. Common-mode behaviour follows ISO 11898-2. A
high-voltage fault-tolerant version runs on SCL or IHP. Second factory run.
9.6 Chip 6 · Voltage supervisor
What it is. Comparators that cancel their own drift. Resistor dividers matched to 0.1 %. An 8
microsecond filter to ignore switching noise. A temperature-stable reference accurate to 10 parts
per million per degree. And a watchdog timer that checks the processor is still alive.

What it replaces. Supervisor chips from Texas Instruments and Maxim. We estimate 30 to 80
million units a year, because nearly every circuit board has one or more. $0.2 to $0.8 commercially,
and 10 to 100 times that screened. Why this process. Accuracy from −40 °C to +125 °C comes
from a trimmed reference and matched resistors. Both are strengths of an older process. Where
it sells, and how many. Every avionics box and every drone module. This chip has the highest
number of sockets in our whole range. Why it goes first. It is the simplest chip we build, so it
carries the MIL-883 screening process for everything behind it. §10 explains that decision. Status.
The noise filter is the design story: ignore switching noise without slowing a real fault response
below 8 microseconds. First or second factory run.
9.7 Chip 7 · 4D radar front end
What it is. 77 and 24 GHz radar, using frequency-sweep detection. Two transmit and four receive
channels. A high-frequency SiGe chip for the radio part, and a 130 nm CMOS chip for the digital
part. The boundary is at the analogue-to-digital converter.

What it replaces. Imported 77 GHz radio front-end chips and the digital chips that go with them.
Why this process, and the hard limit. This chip cannot be built on ordinary CMOS. The IHP
process provides the high-speed transistors that real 77 GHz radar uses. This is the one place
in our range where the process choice is physics, not economics. Where it sells, and how many.
We estimate 2 to 8 million units a year in Indian car and security radar at $8 to $25 each, plus
our own AD2 platform and defence radar from FY28. The legal or demand hook. The defence
ministry lists radar warning receivers for Su-30 MKI and Mi-17 aircraft, weapon-locating radar,

What it replaces. Imported zonal controllers and gateway chips that bridge older car networks to
Ethernet. Why this process. A gateway is about how many channels it has and how predictable its
timing is. It is not about clock speed. The network standard bounds the delay in the switch, not
in the processor. Where it sells, and how many. We estimate 4 to 12 million units a year in Indian

old relay-and-wiring-harness box. That is a cost and weight saving the car maker argues for on
your behalf. What it does not do. 130 nm at 200 MHz handles the local layer, not the central

unit and fast memory. That is a much smaller process, and we do not claim it anywhere in this
document. 9.10 Track B · D100 drone chip What it is. Flight control, plus position tracking

chunks.section: 10.1 What ₹40–80 L per chip actually buys
chunks.text:
DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
10.1 What ₹40–80 L per chip actually buys
Approval is not one test. For a commercial industrial chip it is a defined sequence with a defined
number of samples. For a screened defence chip it is longer. Characterisation means measuring
the chip across manufacturing variation, voltage and temperature, on enough units to write a
datasheet with real limits instead of simulated ones. Reliability means hightemperature life testing,
temperature cycling, humidity, static-discharge and latch-up testing. And for defence versions,
screening means burn-in, electrical testing at temperature extremes, leak testing on the package
seal, and the paperwork trail that MIL-883, JSS and CEMILAC approval require. The reliability
and screening steps take calendar time. More money does not make them shorter. Five of the
eight steps to a screened chip are in that category. This is why the plan sends commercial chips
first, and pushes chip 6 through the process early — specifically to learn where it slows down
before four other chips are queued behind it. One factory run cannot approve a chip, and that
costs money. A shared run gives you one set of wafers, usually made at typical settings. An
approval needs material from more than one batch, so that batch-tobatch variation is included
in the samples. A defence screening process will ask for it. So ₹40–80 L per chip is honestly a
commercial-grade approval figure. A screened version needs extra material, and for the analogue
chips that means extra factory runs, not just extra test time. We have sized the round for four
approvals rather than seven for exactly this reason, and §13 names the three that are not funded.

PART FIVE
Two ways to sell the same chip, and why nobody can copy us The commercial route is self-service.
The defence route is relationship-led and protected by law. One ap- proved chip, two prices 10 to
100 times apart. And a big competitor with no available answer.
11 Two ways to sell the same chip
Selling chips is not a pitch. It is a sequence of things you hand the customer. A design engineer
downloads a datasheet, decides in ten minutes whether the chip can work, buys an evaluation
board with a credit card, gets it running in a week, and only then does anyone discuss commercial
terms. If any item in that chain is missing, the process stops there, no matter how good the silicon
is.

That is why ₹1.0 Cr of the round is sales and working capital. And it is why the distributor
conversation matters more than it looks. A catalogue chip that is not in stock and cannot be
found in a search does not exist to the engineer who needs it. The defence route works differently.
You find the item on SRIJAN or a PIL. You have a technical discussion with the defence company.
You supply trial units. You get a Make-II or direct order. Then you go on the approved-vendor
list. The trial stage is where a small company wins, because the buyer is risking time rather than
money, and an Indian-designed part beats an import before price is discussed. Both routes use
the same approved chip, at prices 10 to 100 times apart. That is the real eﬀiciency of having a
range, and it is why low volume is still good business here.
11.1 What we found when we read the government lists ourselves
We read the defence ministry’s 5th PIL — 346 items, scanned, so we had to run text recognition
on it — and DMA lists 1, 2, 3 and 5, directly rather than relying on summaries. What we found
was not what we expected, and it changed how we sell. The lists name boxes, not chips. They
list swappable units, assemblies and spare parts. Most of PIL-5 is bushes, valves, pumps, gaskets
and optical filters. There is no chip-level item anywhere in what we read.

14.1 The seven things we would fix first, in order of value
1. Publish what the 130 nm test chip actually cost, and what was on it. This is the correction
we least wanted and most needed. The whole cost argument in §2 rests on a ₹0.6–1.2 Cr figure
that has never been done once. Except that we have already made a chip on this method, so
a real number exists and we are simply not showing it. It either supports the claim or it does
not, and either way a reader is entitled to it before being asked to trust the estimate. It also
answers the question behind it: did that chip contain any analogue? 2. Run the timing analysis
on sky130 and publish it, per chip. The 200 MHz number is the biggest claim we make and it is
currently a design target. One report per chip turns it into a fact, and it is the cheapest credibility
available to us. 3. Get the production price quote in writing. Our factory service has said it is
willing to support a direct production route. Their published FAQ still says prototypes only. A
quoted mask set and first wafer batch turns the whole production half of this plan from a verbal
indication into a number. That is the difference between a company that can invoice in FY27 and
one that cannot. 4. Get the BEL electronic-warfare specification. It unlocks the highest-value
matches on the government lists, and settles the SiGe-versus-CMOS question that gates the whole
chip 7 family. 5. Replace target numbers with measured numbers. When the first 130 nm batch
comes back, swap in real coverage, timing, yield and test results for the current targets. Every
drawing in this document is built to accept that swap without being redrawn. That one change
turns a plan

DEEPGRID SEMI | Mature-Node Silicon for India’s Defence and Industrial Base
PLAIN EDITION · CONFIDENTIAL
14.2
Where we could fool ourselves — the audit we ran on our own plan
We checked this plan for wishful thinking using investor Charlie Munger’s famous checklist —
the way we would tear apart somebody else’s pitch. The core survives: the ten-times cost cut is
arithmetic; ₹2.88 crore of orders is fact; the import bans are real. Four kinds of wishful thinking
had crept in, and each one changed this document:
• Borrowed glory. We quoted other companies’ huge order books in ways that made them
sound like our orders. Fixed — they are labelled as the size of the door, and our money moves
only on our own signed letters.
• Permission mistaken for orders. A list entry is permission, not an order. Fixed — the
three buyer speeds in §11.2, each with its own clock.
• Protecting our own number. Our forecast added to exactly ₹1,000 crore in every revision
— a sign we were protecting the number. Fixed — the crash-price table now travels with it
everywhere.
• One skill mistaken for another. Being good at chips is not being good at supporting three
hundred customers. Fixed — the support-engineer team is a funded line.
When everything pushes one way: national pride, government deadlines, finished docu-
ments and exciting tender numbers all push the same direction — build more, faster. When
every force in the room points one way, that is itself the warning. Our defence is the rule, the
scoreboard, and the stop rules — written calmly, in advance.

LVDS/DSI in · SXGA @ 60 Hz · 1280 × 10-bit column DACs · 0–12 V HV amps · temp-compensated gamma · frame-freeze BIST (ASIL-B capable).
The policy anchor
PIL-5 line item: BEL 17-inch rugged SXGA display, due Dec 2027 — a named DPSU socket with a 
date, cited from DDP's 5th list on the sheet itself.
Replaces
Novatek/Himax-class TCON + source-driver imports in defence MFDs, industrial HMI, rail PIS and 
automotive clusters — 2–6M/yr sockets at $3–12.
Why 130 nm wins
HV output amps (0–12 V swing, thick oxide) and 24 V gate-driver level shift are mature-node 
territory; charge-sharing precharge cuts driver power ~40%. Cycle-3 MPW.

SDV Zonal Controller + Gateway
ASIL-D lockstep island · EVITA-full HSM + secure boot/OTA · TSN switch (802.1Qbv/AS) · CAN-FD×8, CAN-XL, LIN×8, FlexRay · smart fuse ×16.
Scope honesty (on-sheet)
130 nm at 200 MHz owns the ZONAL layer — gateway, smart I/O, safety and security edge. Central 
SDV compute (multi-GHz, GPU/NPU, LPDDR5) is sub-10 nm and explicitly NOT claimed.
Socket & market

addressable, zonal layer only — flagged internal estimate.
Where it fits
Bridges the CV ADAS heritage (AD2) and the DG SDV platform: this is the mature-node edge of the 
same architecture Design.png shows at the centre.

D 1 0 0
Drone SoC D100 — Phase 2, the Revenue-Now Silicon
Flight control (PX4/ArduPilot loop) + visual-inertial odometry (EKF pose 30 Hz) + optional 10-TOPS NPU — with a hardware failsafe island independent of the mission stack.
The wedge (on-sheet)
Failsafe island in hardware, not firmware: link monitor → safe-state FSM → 
independent path direct to ESC, isolated power and clock — bypasses FC, VIO 
and AI. DGCA type-certification path.
Market (sheet, cited)
India drone market $1.2–1.3B → $2.7–3.2B by ’30–34; SoC ASP $100–800; 
ideaForge guided 340–450 units in Q4 FY26 alone. No indigenous FC+VIO SoC 
exists — gap stated with references.
Status
FPGA prototype validates; product is 130 nm at 200 MHz fixed. VIO is 
geometry, not learned perception — survives GPS jamming (LoC/LAC use 
case).

DG SDV Platform — The Architecture Behind It All
Deepgrid’s platform reference: secure + safe (triple-lockstep) + Linux host (RV64GCH) + vector & integer accelerator domains on a 64-bit AXI4 matrix with AXI-REALM QoS.
SKU-9 is the mature-node zonal edge of this platform; the D100 is its airborne sibling; SKU-3 powers, SKU-6 supervises, SKU-5 connects — one architecture, many dies.

Wire-bonded mature dies + one flip-chip 28 nm compute die on a 4-layer organic substrate — mature-node packaging at mature-node cost.
Package summary
4-layer organic substrate · BGA 15×15 · wire-bond ×6 + flip-chip 
×1 · die-to-die SPI/UART/GPIO over substrate · power tree from 
SKU-3 · SKU-6 supervises the package · deliberately not UCIe.

The 28 nm AI-compute die (D100 core) joins after the ₹50 Cr

chunks.text:
R O A D M A P
Node & SKU Roadmap — Three Phases, Arithmetic-Checked
130/180 nm ships the catalogue; 90/55/45 nm takes the logic-bound parts from 2028; 28 nm takes compute from 2030 — with the honest boundary and the SKU-ramp correction printed on the figure.
Phase 2 · why shrink at all
Channel count and DSP throughput — not speed vanity: GNSS baseband (90/55), SDR 
transceiver (SiGe+CMOS), drone nav co-processor (55/45). Analog IO rings stay 130 
nm where voltage and ESD demand it.
Phase 3 · the honest boundary
“Everything above is a sub-10 nm problem. 28 nm buys some of it. None of it is 
claimable on 130 nm, at any clock.” — printed on the roadmap itself.
The arithmetic check
The figure corrects its own draft: 10 SKUs/yr and 1,000 SKUs by Year 5 were 
inconsistent by 20×. Shown ramp: ~50-SKU catalogue by Year 5 — one number, before 
an investor finds two.
